welder.intro: Learn welding from the ground up — safety, metal preparation, technique, and quality. A career that pays well, travels well, and never goes out of demand in a growing economy.

skillDomains.name: Workshop Safety
skillDomains.description: Welding kills careless people. Safety is the first skill, not an afterthought.

skills.name: Personal Protective Equipment
skills.description: The gear that stands between you and serious injury.

modules.title: Why welders wear armour
modules.content:
Welding produces:

  • Ultraviolet light that burns eyes and skin (arc eye is a real injury)
  • Molten metal spatter at 1,500°C+
  • Toxic fumes from flux and coatings
  • Noise from grinding and cutting

Every piece of PPE exists because someone got hurt without it. Wear all of it, every time. No exceptions — not even for a 30-second tack weld.

modules.title: The full PPE checklist
modules.content:
Head and face

  • Welding helmet with correct shade lens (auto-darkening is best)
  • Safety glasses underneath (for chipping slag)
  • Cap under helmet if you have long hair

Body

  • Leather welding jacket or apron
  • Long sleeves, no cuffs (spatter catches in cuffs)
  • Leather gauntlet gloves

Feet

  • Steel-toe leather boots, high-top
  • No open shoes, ever

Respiratory

  • Respirator if welding galvanised, painted, or stainless steel
  • Good ventilation always

steps.q: You're about to tack weld a small joint. Can you skip the helmet?
o: Only if the weld is very small
Only if you close your eyes
steps.f: Arc eye can happen from a single flash. Never skip the helmet.

steps.q: You're welding galvanised steel. What extra protection is required?
steps.f: Galvanised coating releases toxic zinc fumes.

steps.q: You notice your welding jacket sleeve has a hole. What do you do?
steps.f: A hole in leather lets spatter through.

modules.title: Safety assessment for a new site
modules.prompt: You've been hired to weld a metal gate on a client's property. Describe how you assess the site for safety before starting work.
modules.context: Every new site is a new hazard.
rubric: Checks for flammable materials nearby (wood, fuel, cloth)
Checks ventilation or whether outdoor welding is possible
Checks electrical supply and grounding
Checks for bystanders (especially children)
Prepares a fire extinguisher or water bucket
Notes emergency exits and phone signal
Confirms weather conditions (wind can spread spatter)

skills.name: Fire Prevention
skills.description: Welding sparks travel far. Preventing fires is part of the job.

modules.title: Sparks travel farther than you think
modules.content:
Welding spatter can travel up to 10 metres and stay hot enough to ignite wood, cloth, or fuel for minutes after landing.

Before welding anywhere

  1. Clear a 10-metre radius of anything flammable
  2. Cover what can't be moved with fire blankets
  3. Have a fire extinguisher within arm's reach
  4. Have a bucket of water or sand nearby
  5. Never weld near fuel, gas cylinders, or paint

After welding, stay on site for at least 30 minutes. Smouldering fires take time to show.

modules.title: React to a fire
modules.prompt: You're welding in a client's workshop. Sparks have ignited a small fire in a pile of rags 3 metres away. Walk through exactly what you do.
modules.context: Small fires become large fires in under 60 seconds.
rubric: Stops welding immediately and turns off equipment
Assesses whether it's small enough to fight or needs evacuation
Uses correct extinguisher type (dry powder or CO2 for electrical areas)
Aims at the base of the fire, not the flames
Evacuates if the fire grows or smoke becomes thick
Calls for help and clears other people away
Reports to client and documents the incident

skillDomains.name: Metal Preparation
skillDomains.description: A weld is only as good as the preparation.

skills.name: Reading Drawings
skills.description: Interpret technical drawings and welding symbols.

modules.title: Drawings are a language
modules.content:
Before you cut a single piece of metal, you must read the drawing. A drawing tells you:

  • Dimensions of every piece
  • Type of weld required at each joint
  • Materials and thickness
  • Any special notes

Misreading a drawing wastes metal and time.

modules.title: The five welding symbols you must know
modules.content:
1. Fillet weld (triangle)

The most common weld. Joins two pieces at a right angle.

2. Butt weld (straight line)

Joins two pieces end-to-end or edge-to-edge.

3. Square butt

Simple edge-to-edge without bevel.

4. V-groove (V shape)

Pieces are beveled to allow deeper penetration.

5. Weld-all-around (circle at joint)

Means weld the entire circumference or perimeter.

Numbers next to symbols indicate leg length or weld size in millimetres.

steps.q: A drawing shows a triangle with a '6' next to it at a corner joint. What does this mean?
steps.f: Triangle = fillet weld. The number indicates leg length in mm.

steps.q: A symbol shows a circle at the joint between two pieces. What does this mean?
steps.f: The circle at the joint (weld-all-around) means weld the full perimeter.

steps.q: A drawing shows a V shape at the joint. Why is the V there?
o: The pieces are beveled to allow deeper weld penetration
steps.f: A V-groove is prepared so the weld penetrates the full thickness.

skills.name: Cleaning & Fit-Up
skills.description: Clean metal welds well. Dirty metal welds badly.

modules.title: The invisible enemy: contamination
modules.content:
Weld contamination comes from:

  • Rust
  • Mill scale (the dark coating on new steel)
  • Oil and grease
  • Paint
  • Moisture

All of these cause:

  • Porosity (holes in the weld)
  • Poor penetration
  • Cracking
  • Weak joints

Clean metal is the foundation of a strong weld. There are no shortcuts here.

steps.q: You receive newly cut steel from the supplier. First step?
o: Clean edges of mill scale, rust, and oil
steps.f: New steel has mill scale and cutting oils.

steps.q: There's light surface rust on the joint area. What do you do?
o: Grind or wire-brush to bare metal

steps.q: After cleaning, the two pieces don't fit flush. What do you do?
o: Grind or cut to fit properly
Use more weld to fill the gap
steps.f: Fit-up before welding. Gaps cause distortion and weak joints.

skillDomains.name: Welding Techniques
skillDomains.description: The core skill: joining metal with heat and filler.

skills.name: Arc Welding (SMAW)
skills.description: Stick welding — the workhorse of West African workshops.

modules.title: What is arc welding?
modules.content:
Arc welding (also called stick welding or SMAW — Shielded Metal Arc Welding) uses an electrical arc between a consumable electrode and the metal to create heat and melt both the electrode and the workpiece together.

Why it's everywhere in West Africa

  • Equipment is cheap and durable
  • Works outdoors, in wind and rain
  • No gas cylinders needed
  • One machine handles many metals

If you can arc weld well, you can find work anywhere.

modules.title: Setting the machine
modules.content:
Amperage by electrode diameter

  • 2.5mm electrode → 70–90A
  • 3.2mm electrode → 100–130A
  • 4.0mm electrode → 130–180A
  • 5.0mm electrode → 180–240A

By metal thickness

  • Thin sheet (1–2mm) → lower amps, 2.5mm rod, faster travel
  • Medium (3–6mm) → 3.2mm rod, moderate amps
  • Thick (6mm+) → 4.0mm+ rod, high amps, may need multiple passes

Get amperage wrong and: too low = sticking rod, no penetration. Too high = burn-through, spatter, undercut.

steps.q: The electrode keeps sticking to the workpiece. Most likely cause?
steps.f: Low amperage doesn't create enough heat to keep the arc going.

steps.q: You see 'undercut' — a groove melted into the base metal beside the weld. Cause?
o: Amperage too high or travel too fast
steps.f: Undercut comes from too much heat input or moving too fast.

steps.q: The weld has small holes in it (porosity). What's the most likely cause?

modules.title: Weld a critical joint
modules.prompt: You need to weld a 6mm steel plate butt joint that will carry significant load. Describe your approach — preparation, settings, technique, and post-weld inspection.
modules.context: Structural welds must be correct. The consequences of failure are injury or death.
rubric: Cleans and bevels the joint edges
Sets machine for 3.2mm or 4.0mm rod at correct amps
Tacks the joint first to prevent distortion
Runs a root pass, then fill passes if needed
Maintains consistent travel speed and angle
Inspects for porosity, undercut, cracks
May consider a cap pass for appearance and strength

modules.title: Build a weld sample library
modules.prompt: Produce and photograph at least 5 weld samples showing: butt joint, fillet joint, T-joint, lap joint, and corner joint. Label each with technique and settings.
steps: Write a note on what was hard/easy about each

skills.name: Joint Types
skills.description: The five fundamental joints every welder must master.

modules.title: The five joints
modules.content:
1. Butt joint

Two pieces end-to-end. Used for lengthening, repairing.

2. Corner joint

Two pieces meeting at 90° forming an L. Used for boxes, frames.

3. T-joint

One piece perpendicular to another. Used for structural frameworks.

4. Lap joint

Two pieces overlapping. Used for sheet metal, panels.

5. Edge joint

Two pieces joined along their edges. Used for thin sheet.

Every welded structure is a combination of these five.

steps.q: You're welding the corner of a steel box. Which joint?
You're welding a cross-beam onto a truck chassis frame. Which joint?
You're repairing a crack in a metal fuel tank (empty and purged). Which joint?
steps.f: Filling a crack in a flat surface uses a butt joint.

skillDomains.name: Quality & Business
skillDomains.description: Inspect your work and turn skill into income.

skills.name: Inspection & Quality
skills.description: Judge your own work against real standards.

modules.title: Weld inspection basics
modules.content:
Every weld should be visually inspected before the job is considered done. Look for:

  • Cracks — anything remotely looking like a crack is a rejection
  • Porosity — small holes, indicates contamination
  • Undercut — melted groove beside the weld, weakens the joint
  • Incomplete fusion — weld doesn't stick to the base metal
  • Slag inclusions — trapped slag inside the weld
  • Spatter — cosmetic but unprofessional if excessive

Structural and pressure welds require professional NDT (non-destructive testing) — X-ray, ultrasonic, or dye penetrant.

steps.q: You see a small crack running along the edge of a weld. Action?
steps.f: Any crack is a serious defect. Grind it out completely and re-weld.

steps.q: You see light porosity (small holes) in a non-structural fence weld. Action?
o: Grind and re-weld if time allows; note to client
steps.f: Non-structural porosity is often acceptable, but professional welders still fix it when possible.

steps.q: You see undercut along a structural weld. Action?
o: Grind and re-weld — undercut weakens the joint
steps.f: Undercut reduces the cross-section of the base metal.

skills.name: Estimating & Pricing
skills.description: Quote jobs correctly and never lose money on a weld.

modules.title: How to price a welding job
modules.content:
Every welding quote covers:

  1. Materials — steel, electrodes, gas, consumables
  2. Labour — your time at a real hourly rate
  3. Overhead — electricity, transport, tool wear
  4. Profit — the margin that keeps you in business

Most beginner welders only quote materials + a little. Then they wonder why they're broke.

Price = (Materials + Labour + Overhead) × (1 + Margin)

A 25–40% margin is standard for small fabrication work.
